topic: GLP-1 receptor agonists as a neuroprotective, disease-modifying therapy in Parkinson's disease
biorxiv_note: The available bioRxiv MCP (search_preprints) supports only category + date-range browsing, not keyword/full-text search. Scanned the 30 most recent preprints (up to 365-day window) in each of the three most plausible categories -- neuroscience, pharmacology and toxicology, and physiology -- and found no preprint specifically addressing GLP-1 receptor agonists in Parkinson's disease. This is reported as a genuine null result of the available tool, not a claim that no such bioRxiv preprints exist.

findings.claim: GLP-1 receptor agonists exert anti-inflammatory, neurotrophic, and neuroprotective effects in preclinical models of neurodegeneration, motivating their repurposing from type 2 diabetes treatment to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

source.title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and neuroinflammation: Implications for neurodegenerative disease treatment.
source.authors: Kopp KO, Glotfelty EJ, Li Y, Greig NH

findings.claim: In a single-center phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=62), once-weekly exenatide 2mg for 48 weeks improved off-medication MDS-UPDRS part III motor scores by an adjusted mean difference of -3.5 points versus placebo (95% CI -6.7 to -0.3; p=0.0318), an effect sustained through a 12-week washout period.

source.title: Exenatide once weekly versus placebo in Parkinson's disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
source.authors: Athauda D, Maclagan K, Skene SS, et al.

findings.claim: In a phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (LIXIPARK, n=156), daily subcutaneous lixisenatide for 12 months resulted in an MDS-UPDRS part III score change of -0.04 (improvement) versus +3.04 (worsening) with placebo (difference 3.08; 95% CI 0.86-5.30; p=0.007). Nausea occurred in 46% and vomiting in 13% of the lixisenatide group.

source.title: Trial of Lixisenatide in Early Parkinson's Disease.
source.authors: Meissner WG, Remy P, Giordana C, et al.

findings.claim: Across observational, clinical trial, and pooled-analysis evidence, GLP-1 receptor agonists show promising but still preliminary neuroprotective signals for major neurocognitive disorders (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and other dementias), acting through proposed mechanisms including brain energy homeostasis, neuroinflammation, proteostasis, and blood-brain barrier dynamics. Key open questions include brain penetrance, response biomarkers, long-term safety, and cost/availability.

source.title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists for major neurocognitive disorders.
source.authors: De Giorgi R, Ghenciulescu A, Yotter C, Taquet M, Koychev I

findings.claim: A phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Exenatide-PD3, n=194, UK, 96 weeks) found NO evidence that once-weekly exenatide slows Parkinson's disease progression: off-medication MDS-UPDRS III scores worsened by 5.7 points with exenatide versus 4.5 points with placebo (adjusted coefficient 0.92; 95% CI -1.56 to 3.39; p=0.47). This directly follows and complicates the earlier positive phase 2 signal (F2).
findings.provenance_note: NOT found by the initial manual PubMed search (which was sorted by relevance and dated from 2021, missing this Feb 2025 publication). Added after the research swarm's live web search surfaced it (via neurologylive.com, citing the Lancet paper) and PubMed was used to verify the claim wasn't a hallucination. Recorded here for fairness in the swarm-vs-manual comparison, and to correct the original manual report, which is now stale on this point.

source.title: Exenatide once a week versus placebo as a potential disease-modifying treatment for people with Parkinson's disease in the UK: a phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
source.authors: Vijiaratnam N, Girges C, Auld G, et al. (Foltynie T, senior author)

findings.claim: In an MPTP-induced mouse model of Parkinson's disease, the GLP-1/GIP dual agonist tirzepatide reduced dopaminergic neuron loss and improved mitochondrial function (increased ATP, improved mitochondrial ultrastructure) by inhibiting Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission and promoting Pink1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy; a one-third dose of tirzepatide was statistically comparable to semaglutide and levodopa. GLP1R and GIPR expression were also found downregulated in dopaminergic neurons from PD patients (GSE238129 dataset).

source.title: GLP-1/GIP dual agonist tirzepatide alleviates mice model of Parkinson's disease by promoting mitochondrial homeostasis.
source.authors: Tian R, Liu K, Lai H, Liao C, Li J, Tu H

cross_cutting_synthesis_points: Two independent phase 2 RCTs (exenatide, lixisenatide) both showed statistically significant slowing of motor progression on the same primary endpoint (MDS-UPDRS III), with effect sizes in a similar range (~3-3.5 points) -- a notable convergence across different molecules and trial designs.
GI side effects (nausea, vomiting) are consistently reported as the main tolerability issue across trials, consistent with the drug class's known profile in diabetes/obesity use.

Mechanistic evidence has evolved from broad anti-inflammatory/neurotrophic framing (2022 review) to specific, testable pathways -- e.g., mitochondrial fission/mitophagy (2025 tirzepatide study) -- suggesting the field is moving from correlation to mechanism.

Both clinical trials are explicitly framed as insufficient on their own: authors call for larger/longer trials before treatment guidelines could change; this caveat should appear in any faithful summary of the topic.
No bioRxiv preprint was discoverable for this specific topic via the available category/date-browsing tool; PubMed (peer-reviewed, indexed) is the sole practical source for this comparison.

The initial manual PubMed pass missed the most recent and arguably most important data point (F6, the Feb 2025 phase 3 exenatide failure) -- it was found via the research swarm's live web search during the comparison run and then verified against PubMed. This is a real limitation of a single relevance-sorted PubMed query versus live web search for catching the newest publications, and is disclosed here rather than silently patched over.
